conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in today from the GI clinic because of severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain is constant, all over my belly, and it’s been above 10 out of 10 for weeks. Nothing at home helps—especially not the morphine. Only IV Dilaudid gives any relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned nausea and vomiting too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, constant nausea. I stopped my TPN three weeks ago because it made me sicker, but the nausea didn’t go away. I’ve lost about 20 pounds since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. We’ll get you started on hospital TPN to help with nutrition. We also want to manage your pain better. We’ll consult the chronic pain team to help adjust your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just need something that works. I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. We’ll do everything we can. For now, we’ll keep you on your current meds and monitor your labs and vitals closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your albumin is 3.0, which is low but better than the 2.0 from outside. Your hemoglobin is 10.9, so no active bleeding. We’ve started you on IV TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the TPN going to make me nauseous again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using a different formula than your home one—closer to what you’ve tolerated in the hospital before. We’ll monitor you closely and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll give it a try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chronic pain team met with you yesterday. Starting today, we’re increasing your gabapentin to 900 mg three times a day and amitriptyline to 100 mg at night. We’re also starting a Dilaudid PCA pump for 24 hours to see if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried so many things. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to find what works best for you. The PCA lets you control the dose safely. We’ll reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You mentioned new pain and swelling on your left thigh this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s tender and hard. I’ve had cords there from Lovenox shots, but this feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ordering an ultrasound to check for a clot or other issue. Given your anticoagulation, we’re concerned about a hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. No DVT, which is good. But there are two fluid collections in your thigh—could be abscesses or hematomas. You’re not febrile, so infection seems less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery reviewed it and recommends conservative care—warm compresses, lidocaine patches, and monitoring. We’ve held your Lovenox for now because your factor Xa level was high—suggesting you were over-anticoagulated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not on Lovenox anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched to a lower, prophylactic dose—40 mg once daily—since you have a history of DVTs. This balances bleeding and clotting risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your thigh swelling is already a bit smaller today. Pain improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the warm and cold packs help, and the lidocaine patch too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that up. Your nausea has also improved—from constant to about 3 out of 10. You’re tolerating clear liquids well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the nausea is better. The TPN isn’t making me sick, which is a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried the Fentanyl patch yesterday, but you said it made you feel strange?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I felt foggy and had bad thoughts—like I didn’t want to be here. I know it’s not safe, so I told the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for speaking up. We stopped the patch because of your history with suicidal ideation on opioids. We’ve switched to buprenorphine, but you said it didn’t help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No relief at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re now starting methadone 5 mg twice daily. It may help where others haven’t. We’ll monitor closely for side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try anything at this point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped to 8.4, but it’s stable now. We’re attributing it to chronic anemia from malabsorption. You’re on iron, and we’ll check your CBC after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. It’s been low before. We’re watching it, and your primary doctor will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The TPN company has replicated the hospital formula for your home use. You’ll restart it at home with the new mix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it works. I can’t afford to lose more weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is still significant, but methadone seems to be helping a bit. The chronic pain team feels it’s the best option now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not perfect, but better than nothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also starting a lidocaine patch for your leg pain and ketoconazole cream for a groin rash you mentioned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My skin’s been itchy too—any idea why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be from dryness or Sjogren’s. We’re keeping Benadryl available if it bothers you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well overall. The hematoma is shrinking, your pain is more manageable, and you’re tolerating nutrition. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What changes will I have at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on methadone twice daily instead of morphine, gabapentin and amitriptyline at higher doses, and Lovenox 40 mg once daily. We’re switching from vancomycin to ethanol dwell for your catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the ethanol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps prevent infections and works better with your TPN. The home team will show you how.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also want to check your CBC the day after discharge. Your hemoglobin was low, so we need to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still in pain, but it’s better than when I came in. I’m glad to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve made several medication changes. Let me go over them again so you’re clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on methadone for pain, higher doses of gabapentin and amitriptyline, and Lovenox once daily. You’ll use the ethanol catheter dwell and the new TPN formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lidocaine patch for my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, apply it at night for 12 hours. The thigh bruise is healing but may take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if pain worsens, you develop fever, or the leg swelling returns. Follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll send your discharge instructions and prescriptions to your home team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest at home and keep up with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re improving. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep those appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Let us know if anything comes up before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s our job. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.
